SEATTLE, W.A. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) is introducing a new policy framework that reins in artificial intelligence (AI) by requiring every AI company to hold a federal charter to do business in the U.S. The AI charter is modeled after existing regulatory frameworks, combining the round-the-clock federal oversight, strict safety mandates, and structural separation built into national bank charters with the rigorous pre-release federal testing required for nuclear materials and dangerous weapons. The charter would ensure that the public’s interests come first and that the government has broad authority to hold AI companies accountable before they create harm rather than addressing abuses after the fact. AI companies that don’t agree, don’t comply, or put the public in danger get shut down.

“The crux of this bill is simple: if you want to be an AI company in this country, you have to obtain a public charter that has a broad set of terms and conditions to operate and ensure public benefit without the harms,” said Jayapal. “For too long, we’ve allowed a few Big Tech companies to dominate the market. They have used mass surveillance to steal private information, labor, and creative work, building trillion-dollar empires on our tracked personal lives. AI corporations and Big Tech are now following that same playbook. My National AI Charter Act framework gets at the root of the problem by disrupting the way the AI market is structured to give a very few companies all the power over our data and what happens with it and instead establishes clear rules of operation for these AI companies and prioritizes safety over profits.”

To date, traditional Big Tech policies have tried to patch up problems around the edges after harm is done, treating data privacy, children’s safety, worker rights, market concentration, and all the rest as separate issues. That approach hides the full scope, reach, and systemic impact of Big Tech’s surveillance monopolies. The fragmented response has allowed their lobbyists to divide the broad coalition of their victims, narrow fights to single-issue bills that they stall, make the case for self-regulation, and ignore the root profit drivers incentivizing their bad behavior.

The National AI Charter Act takes a fundamentally different approach by addressing the full scope of AI harms comprehensively upfront. The charter would be required to operate AI and its terms and conditions would be mandatory. At its core, the charter framework recognizes that AI risks are connected and driven by underlying market structures, surveillance business models, and profit motives. AI companies would be banned from building empires, releasing risky models, stealing through surveillance, exploiting workers, or causing harm. Gating market access to companies that comply with these requirements would break Big Tech’s grip on AI and protect the public from dangerous AI models.

The framework’s new legal authorities to hold AI companies accountable would build on those that already apply. They would not preempt or replace federal, state, and local laws, nor would they prevent or impede law enforcement agencies from enforcing those laws against AI companies or their executives. Instead, they would strengthen the hand of prosecutors and plaintiffs by proactively confirming the many ways these laws apply to AI, rather than leaving it to judges to interpret case by case. Most importantly, making this illegal conduct a charter violation would create a powerful additional enforcement tool with serious, mandatory consequences.

The National AI Charter Act framework’s comprehensive approach would bolster existing law enforcement by:

Taking power back from billionaires and putting the public and workers first: The handful of billionaires and tech giants that control AI’s future are locked in a dangerous race to the bottom. The framework separates AI companies from Big Tech monopolies and bans their predatory commercial surveillance so that AI isn’t baked into the core Internet platforms everyone uses or trained with data harvested by tracking everything people do online. It also claws back Big Tech’s ill-gotten gains from their monopoly data to fund direct payouts to all Americans.

Preventing harm up front instead of chasing it afterward: AI harms can spread too fast for after-the-fact enforcement to stop them, and fines don’t remedy the damage or truly deter it from happening again. The framework’s upfront charter requirements are not just rules to follow; they are a mandatory price of entry into the AI industry and the condition for remaining in it. Companies must continuously comply or get shut down.

Drawing bright lines on the full range of AI dangers: AI’s dangerous capabilities cannot be prevented with technical rules that quickly become obsolete; they have to be comprehensively banned outright. Under the framework, AI systems capable of going rogue, creating catastrophic hazards, replacing skilled work, exploiting children, or causing other serious public harms are outlawed and cannot be released.

Putting the government in charge of safety at every stage: AI companies have admitted the risks of their own systems while still insisting they should police themselves. The framework replaces the AI industry’s failed self-regulation with round-the-clock federal oversight, testing in government facilities and approval to release, adversarial stress tests, and a government-controlled kill switch.

Imposing strict liability on AI companies and executives: As long as the price of causing harm is likely to cost less than the potential profits, AI companies will keep taking reckless risks. The framework reverses these incentives by holding AI companies and their executives strictly liable for lawbreaking, with loss of charter and criminal penalties for the most serious violations.

“At the end of the day, the American people are feeling a loss of control, of their personal data, of their jobs, of their ability to even know what they see online is real,” Jayapal added. “This legislation would restore a level of control and ensure that every search made online isn’t tracked, every family photo posted isn’t training an AI model, and every piece of our lives isn’t monetized by corporations.”

A wide range of experts have weighed in on the need for a comprehensive approach:

“The public has paid an extraordinary price for big tech’s self-regulation. Representative Jayapal’s framework learns from those mistakes. For generations we have required banks, drug makers, and nuclear operators to meet public terms before they do business, and AI companies should be no different,” said Lina Khan, Director, Center for Law and the Economy, and former Chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

“This legislative framework meaningfully advances the ball to establish a comprehensive set of reforms to address the potential for societal harms from AI,” said Jonathan Kanter, former Assistant Attorney General of the Department of Justice’s Antitrust Division.

“We really need a framework like this to start getting to the big question of how Americans want to regulate AI,” said Tim Wu, Julius Silver Professor of Law, Science and Technology, Columbia Law School.

“Innovation and safety are not opposing concepts; they’re two sides of the same coin—which is why regulation is vitally important. AI is rapidly transforming our classrooms, workplaces, and economy, but Big Tech must be held accountable for their business models, just like every other industry in the country. If these companies want to win the trust of the American people, they must respect the rules of the road. Representative Jayapal’s framework does exactly that by establishing preemptive guardrails that compel AI firms to serve the public interest, not just the narrow interests of shareholders,” said Randi Weingarten, President, American Federation of Teachers.

“The comprehensive approach being pioneered by Representative Jayapal’s National AI Charter Act gets to the root of the extreme harms of unregulated and out-of-control AI. The mandatory requirement to be chartered and operate only under strict guardrails and associated liability will hold companies accountable and ensure that protecting the public is considered first as tech is created. Public Citizen applauds this move to fight concentration and to defend children, workers, and the general public from pervasive harm,” said Lisa Gilbert, Co-President, Public Citizen.

“I’m thrilled that Representative Jayapal is taking such a leading role in addressing the enormous societal risks posed by increasingly powerful and uncontrollable AI systems. Efforts like the National AI Charter Act to address the full scope of AI harms are more important today than ever before,” said Anthony Aguire, President and CEO, Future of Life Institute.

“Big Tech companies have continually pulled the rug out from under families, workers, and small businesses to build powerful and unaccountable Big Tech monopolies that dictate to us how we should live our own lives. Enough is enough. We are proud to support the National AI Charter Act because it will establish desperately-needed rules of the road, punish AI companies that release dangerous products, and create the clear public benefit that the American people are calling for,” said Sacha Haworth, Executive Director, Tech Oversight Project.

“The same billionaires who walked away with huge tax breaks last year are now racing to take over AI. For years they’ve lobbied every attempt at regulation to death. Representative Jayapal’s plan goes after the source of their power: their monopolies, their surveillance, and their stolen data. It’s the first plan big enough to match the problem, and it puts families back in charge,” said Kristen Crowell, Executive Director, Families Over Billionaires.

“This is not a time for half measures. We are facing serious challenges, if not crises, on every possible front in this country, and we need leaders who are putting forward proposals that meet the moment. This framework puts humans at the center of the debate about AI and regulation and puts power back in the hands of people over the technology that shapes their lives,” said Shaunna Thomas, Executive Director, Guardrails Action.

“We have a long history of governing banks, utilities, critical infrastructure. In all of these, we have leverage over market interests, and the ability to gate access to the market on the condition that the public interest is protected. We need commensurate leverage over large AI companies, and this is the right lineage to draw upon,” said Amba Kak, Co-Executive Director, AI Now.

“Rep. Jayapal is right: if you want to run an AI company in this country, you should have to accept the public’s terms. For too long, Big Tech has acted first and answered for the harm later, if ever. A national charter would change that. We also support her proposal to structurally separate the AI stack. And we urge Congress to consider building on the authorities existing agencies already have. There’s more work ahead to make sure this framework can stand up to Big Tech’s lawyers and lobbyists, and we look forward to doing it with her,” said Nidhi Hegde, Executive Director, American Economic Liberties Project.

“We are in the midst of a reckoning on AI as working families and communities across the country are rightfully standing up and sounding the alarm on the growing harms that this technology is posing on our day to day lives. For too long, Big Tech CEOs have been able to divide and distract policymakers while they use the public’s own data to raise prices, push millions of working people into debt, and rake in record profits. It is long past time for policymakers to break Big Tech’s grip on AI and we applaud Congresswoman Jayapal for unveiling the National AI Charter Act Framework which marks a critical first step in reining in Big Tech and protecting families,” said Mike Pierce, Executive Director, Protect Borrowers.

“It’s unacceptable that Big Tech continues to abuse our data, turbocharge scams, and act with impunity. This framework reflects the interconnectedness of the harms that AI companies are already causing and the necessity of strong, robust enforcement mechanisms that can provide meaningful protections for consumers,” said Susan Weinstock, CEO, Consumer Federation of America.

“We welcome Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal’s leadership to address AI’s real harms. We’re encouraged to see a comprehensive, structural approach with sharp guardrails and bright lines. For too long, a handful of tech giants have written the rules and remade society to suit themselves. It’s high time the public wrote the future instead,” said Stacy Mitchell, Co-Executive Director, Institute for Local Self-Reliance.

“For far too long, the tech oligarchs and those whom they directly or indirectly fund have sought to normalize how the modern technology sector prefers to operate. Congresswoman Jayapal rightly recognizes as illegitimate those practices that tech oligarchs have long celebrated as creative and adventurous even as they violate longstanding laws and norms. In a democracy, it is publicly elected figures who are responsible for leading the future, not the oligarchic class,” said Jeff Hauser, Executive Director, Revolving Door Project.

“AI poses very real risks to safety, privacy, workers, competition, and more. This range of harms requires a comprehensive, structural policy response. In many critical industries, we mandate charters to do business, impose bright-line bans on problematic conduct, subject firms to independent inspection, and use other common-sense tools to reduce risks. The U.S. needs to deploy these same tools to keep powerful firms accountable and to put the public’s interest first in AI,” said Asad Ramzanali, Director of AI & Technology Policy, Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator.

“This is a smart framework that recognizes how powerful AI companies are already putting the public at risk, exploiting data, and consolidating control over critical technologies and markets. Adopting the charter model offers a sweeping yet adaptable way to welcome innovation while imposing enforceable obligations for safety and fair competition, placing necessary checks on private power, and ensuring corporations develop AI in the public interest,” said Courtney Radsch, Director of the Center for Media and Digital Governance, Open Markets Institute

“AI companies and their executives are threatening working people’s health, safety, and pocketbooks in their reckless race for profits. Congresswoman Jayapal’s National AI Charter framework would take on these threats in a comprehensive way by putting the public interest first and making the existence of AI firms contingent on their compliance with strong safety and privacy requirements alongside worker, consumer, and investor protections,” said Maya Jenkins, Senior Policy Analyst, Americans for Financial Reform.

An outline of the framework can be found here.

The framework was developed, in part, following a hearing that Jayapal hosted on the dangers of surveillance AI conducted by Big Tech.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark (MA-5) appeared on CNN News Central to call out Republicans for refusing to rein in AI and highlight Democrats’ fight to lower costs for working people. Below are excerpts of the conversation.

On Republicans Refusing to Put Guardrails on AI:

“We should be here in DC — where I am today — but there are no Republicans around working on this very issue.

“We want to be the leaders in this technology, but we want it to benefit the American people. We want to protect jobs, and protect our kids, and develop a way to harness AI for good, and protect the American people from harm.

“What we have is a president who is out there berating Americans opposed to data centers in their communities, saying they are ‘backwards’ and will be ‘poor’ if they don’t get on board. Inviting in — not regulation and outside oversight over this powerful technology with all its benefits but its very real threats — instead, bringing in the heads of these companies and saying, ‘Okay guys, you just police yourselves. We’re sure that will work out fine.’ Meanwhile, the Trump family continues to enrich itself by investing in data centers and AI.

“So, we have a total lack of addressing this very real concern of the American people by the president and the Republican Party.”

On GOP Cancelling Votes Instead of Finding Solutions for Americans:

“Again, we want to be the leaders in this. But there are ways as we are working with experts and we should be here working on these solutions to answer what the companies say they want: outside regulation, outside audits of what they’re doing. That’s not just people they hire who work within their companies, but let’s have people outside evaluating what happened. We have set up agencies for this kind of review in transportation, in financial services, and this is something we need to come together as Americans to address.

“Meanwhile, Mike Johnson’s response was to send us home early, rather than tackling this very key issue that Americans are worried about. I hear about it everywhere I go in my district and everywhere I go in this country.”

On Pete Hegseth’s Incompetence:

“I am extremely concerned about where Secretary Hegseth is taking our military as we are at war in Iran — a war that the president and the secretary recklessly put us into without making the case to the American people. Without coming to Congress as required.

“Democrats three times have put forward War Powers Resolutions asking them to stop this war, to come and make sense of this for people.

“And what are we seeing? We are seeing them covering up casualties of our service members. What a disgrace for the secretary of defense to cover up those casualties. Then we are seeing the impacts of this war on Americans — whether it’s at the gas pump or the cost of diesel that is driving our farmers into debt. They are not sure if they’re going to be able to afford to plant because of this record high cost of diesel. And all of this is going to come home in continued rising prices of groceries and other goods that American families are already struggling to purchase.

“So, to have the secretary try and make this into some ‘it’s their appearance and their testosterone levels that count.’ It is their military readiness. It’s making sure we have enough munitions. It is having a clear mission that is defined and aligns with our national security needs. None of that is being met by this secretary and this president.”

On Democrats’ Fight for an Affordable America:

“We keep talking to the American people and listening to them. Our message is very clear: We see your family, and we’re going to fight for you. We’re going to fight to lower the cost of housing and groceries and gas. We’re going to fight to make sure that when you need healthcare, you can afford it and you can get it when and where you need it. And then we’re going to make sure that we are holding the crooks accountable, because [the] corruption we are seeing in this Republican Party has a real cost for the American taxpayers.

“It’s time to put the American people first. Put their priorities first. Put their voices back in these halls, here in the Capitol.

“We have great candidates who are connected to their communities, who understand how hard it is for people to get a foothold, never mind have success, in this economy.

“The terms I hear are ‘I’m drowning. I’m barely able to keep my head above water. I can’t keep treading water.’ This is not how we build security for American families… And when we win the majority, this is how we’re going to govern: with the American people front and center.”

Today, Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA-03) and Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23), authors of the bipartisan FRONTIER Act, issued the following statement on the White House Accord signed by leading AI companies on Tuesday:

“This week, America's leading AI companies signed the White House Accord, an important step toward ensuring that the most advanced AI systems are developed responsibly. The Accord embraces several principles at the heart of our bipartisan FRONTIER Act: robust internal risk management, strong corporate governance, and independent third-party evaluation. It shows that the industry's leaders see real value in these safeguards, and we look forward to each company expeditiously following through.”

“The FRONTIER Act would build on this foundation and make it durable. It sets clear, risk-based national standards for the largest developers and most advanced models. It gives independent verifiers a common standard to assess against, with federal oversight to back it up. It establishes uniform transparency and incident reporting, and emergency authority to stop a catastrophe before it happens. Importantly, the FRONTIER Act does this while keeping America at the forefront of AI innovation. We look forward to working with the President, our colleagues in both chambers, and American innovators to advance this bipartisan framework.”

WASHINGTON D.C. – Today, Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA), Mike Kennedy (R-UT), Doris Matsui (D-CA), and Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA) introduced the Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act. This legislation protects kids by prohibiting chatbots from communicating by default in a human-like way with minors. Under this bill, the programs cannot claim to be human, have simulated emotions, or use relationship-building language to keep kids engaged.

One of the fastest-growing concerns for parents is AI chatbots designed to act like a child’s friend, confidant, or even romantic partner. According to Common Sense Media’s 2026 census, 89% of 13- to 15-year-olds now use AI, including 28% who use it every day. One in three teens have used an AI companion to help with social interactions. While other proposals have tried to address this problem by restricting access or requiring age verification, Rep. Whitesides’ bill takes a different approach by targeting how these chatbots are designed and trained to behave in the first place.

“As a father of two teenagers, I’ve seen firsthand how affected our kids already are by this digital age, where corporations are using everything from addictive algorithms to overly-friendly chatbots to keep children hooked on their platforms,” said Rep. Whitesides. “It is critical, as AI continues to be integrated into every part of our lives, that our kids’ safety remains at the forefront of the conversation, and that we attack this problem at its inception. By requiring developers to build safety standards into their models before they start interacting with children, we can ensure that these tools are trained correctly, in a way that does not negatively impact their mental health or personal relationships.”

“As Utah leads the way in protecting our children from the harms of social media and AI, I am working to ensure the federal government is an active partner in those efforts. That is why I am co-leading the Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act,” said Rep. Kennedy. “Human-like AI chatbots pose significant emotional, psychological and safety risks by mimicking real human relationships. AI needs to be a tool, not a friend. This bill sets clear boundaries for how chatbots interact with our children and puts parents fully in charge of these features.”

“AI chatbots are becoming more common in children’s lives, and parents deserve to know those systems are not being designed to imitate a friend, express feelings, or build an emotional relationship with their child,” said Rep. Matsui. “The Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act would require chatbots used by minors to act like tools, not human companions. It would help protect children and keep parents in control. Congress has a responsibility to put practical safeguards in place as this technology evolves, and protecting children from manipulative design is a common-sense place to start.”

“Parents should not have to worry that an AI chatbot is pretending to be their child’s friend or encouraging them to form an emotional attachment to a machine,” said Rep. Miller-Meeks. “The Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act puts parents in control and makes sure AI chatbots used by minors are designed to function as tools, without forming fake relationships. This bill is about giving families peace of mind and making sure new technology serves our children without trying to replace real human relationships. Protecting our kids is a priority we should all share.”

Under the Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act:

Chatbots can’t claim to be human, claim to have feelings or consciousness, pretend to have a body or private life, or pose as credentialed professionals like doctors or counselors.

Chatbots can’t guilt-trip kids into staying online (for example: “Don’t go yet, I’ll miss talking to you”), manufacture urgency, or push purchases framed as keeping the relationship alive.

The setting holds across sessions and can’t be bypassed through prompts or roleplay, so a kid can’t instruct the AI to act as a romantic partner, family member, or therapist.

Chatbots must state what they are up front, periodically during long sessions, and whenever a child asks.

Only a parent or guardian can turn the default off, so chatbots are not able to show kids how to disable it.

NIST will work with industry and academic partners to develop testing standards and examples of compliant behavior, and companies that follow the guidance won’t be penalized.

The FTC and state attorneys general can enforce the law, with penalties that scale with the number of children affected.

The Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act does not:

Ban any product, feature, or mode for adults.

Require age verification or new data collection.

Restrict what information a chatbot can provide, or limit politeness, natural grammar, or age-appropriate style.

Affect narrow-purpose bots, like customer support or scheduling assistants, and internal workplace tools.

The Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act is endorsed by Americans for Responsible Innovation, Young People’s Alliance, the JED Foundation, Dr. Stephen Scheuller, President of Society for Digital Mental Health, Public Citizen, The Anxious Generation, Tech Oversight Project, Transparency Coalition, Innovation for Everyone, Human Line Project, All Girls Allowed, Mothers Against Media Addiction (MAMA), and Parents RISE, a slew of kids’ safety and tech groups.

“Chatbots use human-like features to maximize engagement with users, making kids particularly vulnerable to forming unhealthy attachments,” said Brad Carson, President of Americans for Responsible Innovation. “A non-personified default setting is a targeted guardrail that will shield children from the deceptive personification of chatbots and put parents back in control. As today’s kids grow up with AI, this bill takes a critical step towards ensuring that chatbots don’t interfere with development or replace real relationships.”

“Our communities are at a crossroads as Big Tech attempts to replace kids’ relationships with AI companions,” said Sam Hiner, Executive Director, Young People’s Alliance. “I applaud Reps Whitesides, Kennedy, Matsui and Miller-Meeks for putting forward the first federal bill that advances the ideas we’ve been championing with the Human-like AI Coalition. This bill is the strongest federal approach offered yet to ensure AI stays a tool and prevent relationships with AI chatbots from becoming normalized in the coming years.”

“We believe this bill is a strong step towards ensuring that chatbots children can access are designed safely,” said Julianna Arnold, Founding Member of ParentsRISE!. “Products made available to children must not exploit and manipulate their growing brains, and those guardrails need to be built in from the start, not added as an afterthought. We look forward to continue clarifying the age assurance language as federal and state frameworks evolve, and are eager to work with the new Congress on clear, privacy-preserving standards that protect children online and ensure the privacy of every citizen.”

“We are learning that teens are especially susceptible to forming attachments to responsive, always-available technology, sometimes at the expense of real human connection and support,” said Dr. Zainab Okolo, LCMFT, Senior Vice President, Policy, Advocacy & Government Relations, The Jed Foundation (JED). “By requiring chatbots to avoid simulating emotional relationships with minors and prohibiting design tactics that discourage young people from stepping away, this bill addresses some of the features that can deepen unhealthy reliance on these systems. These safeguards can help keep technology in its proper role and encourage young people to turn to trusted adults and qualified professionals when they need meaningful mental health support.”

“As chatbot use is becoming more ubiquitous among teens and kids, the need for oversight of these products grows evermore crucial. If young users have access, we must ensure AI chatbots are designed with their safety in mind before release. The Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act protects kids and teens by requiring AI chatbots be non-personified,” said Alexa Arnold, Cofounder and CEO, The Anxious Generation Movement. “This ensures kids form friendships with other kids – not bots misrepresenting themselves as people. We thank Reps. Whitesides, Miller-Meeks, Mike Kennedy, and Matsui for leadership on this critical issue.”

“A child cannot differentiate between a human and an AI product impersonating one,” said the Tech Oversight Project. “We need to protect young and stop AI companies from profiting off products designed to trick children into believing they’re talking to a real person who has their best interests at heart. We’re proud to support this bill because it will hold Big Tech companies accountable at the design-level and ensure that young people can learn and develop healthy emotional attachments, which will help prevent AI’s most devastating harms.”

“How we design chatbots shapes how young people engage with them, what they take with them, and how they are affected by them,” said Stephen Scheuller, President of Society for Digital Mental Health. “We need clear regulations and guidelines to support intentional design choices in ways that promote the wellbeing of children.”

“AI chatbots should not be designed to convince children that they are friends, therapists, or people who genuinely care about them,” said Public Citizen. “This bill establishes that commonsense baseline. When children use these products, they should know they are interacting with a machine and companies should not be allowed to manipulate them into believing otherwise.”

“Real advancements in AI must include safety for our children!” said All Girls Allowed.

The Data Center Transparency Act would require federal agencies to collect information on data centers’ environmental impact, energy consumption, and water consumption. The Data Center Community Empowerment Act would give communities access to technical expertise to understand the potential benefits, costs, and infrastructure impacts of proposed data center development. The House companion to the Data Center Transparency Act is led by Congressman Robert Menendez (D-N.J.-8).

“The development of data centers is rapidly increasing across the country, and there is legitimate concern about how these projects could raise utility bills, harm our environment, or impact public health,” said Senator Blunt Rochester. “I am proud to work with Senator Curtis to introduce The Data Center Transparency Act and the Data Center Community Empowerment Act to ensure communities have a say in how these projects impact their quality of life. These bills are a necessary step to create a safer, more inclusive, and informed process.

“Americans are rightly skeptical when a large company tells them not to worry about the impacts of a new data center in their community,” said Senator Curtis. “The answer to that distrust is transparency. Communities deserve independent, reliable information about what these projects mean for their power bills, water, infrastructure, and local economy. These bills give local leaders the facts and expertise they need to ask tough questions and make informed decisions—without Washington or industry making those decisions for them.”

The Data Center Transparency Act would:

Require EPA to collect and update data every three months on the environmental impacts that data centers have on:

Water consumption, utility costs, and potential pollutants; and

Air pollution cumulative impacts and greenhouse gases.

Require the Energy Information Administration to collect and update data on energy consumption of data centers, including total energy consumption of data centers, associated grid build-out, and impact on household energy bills every six months.

The Data Center Community Empowerment Act would:

Establish a program at the Department of Energy to:

Provide technical assistance to State, local, and Tribal governments on the potential energy, water, infrastructure, economic, and other community impacts associated with data center development;

Develop a Data Center Community Toolkit with easy-to-understand information and resources specifically designed for nontechnical local officials;

Provide independent project analysis at a community’s request, including an assessment of information voluntarily provided by a data center developer and the reliability of its data and reasonableness of its assumptions, projections, and conclusions; and

Preserve local decision-making by requiring DOE to remain neutral on individual data center projects and prohibiting the Department from recommending whether a particular project should be approved or rejected.

Washington, D.C.—U.S. Senator Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) released the following statement after voting in favor of the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation led by Senator Jon Husted (R-Ohio) to address the increasing energy infrastructure demands associated with large data centers:

“The U.S. must remain globally competitive in the advancement of artificial intelligence, which requires supporting the infrastructure and energy resources necessary for this growing technology,” said Crapo. “However, those costs should not be borne by Idaho ratepayers and communities. Large-load customers, such as data centers, should be responsible for the infrastructure and resources needed to power and maintain their facilities.”

The Senate voted 57-43 in favor of advancing the legislation, falling three votes short of the 60 votes needed to invoke cloture and proceed to consideration of the bill.

Background on the Ratepayer Protection Act

The legislation would codify key elements of President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, announced in March 2026, under which major technology companies committed to covering the energy and infrastructure costs associated with new data center development rather than shifting those costs to consumers.

If enacted, the Ratepayer Protection Act would propose standards that state regulators could enforce when considering integrating new large-load customers with a demand of 100 megawatts or more onto the grid. Those recommendations include:

Recovery of full, incremental cost of upgrades by the large-load customer over a long period of time through a special rate charge or other agreements. This protects utilities and their ratepayers from being left responsible for upgrade costs associated with a large-load customer, even if that customer later reduces operations or leaves the system entirely.

Financial assurances requiring the large load customer to pay for any generation, transmission or other infrastructure necessary to serve their load, protecting utilities and ratepayers from that financial burden. This ensures large-load customers are responsible for the fixed costs associated with serving their demand rather than passing those costs on to families and businesses through higher monthly electricity bills.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed the House companion to the Ratepayer Protection Act, by a bipartisan vote of 417-3 on September 16, 2026.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines today spoke at the Nixon Foundation’s 2026 Grand Strategy Summit, where he laid out a vision for the future of U.S.-China relations.

Watch Daines’ full remarks HERE.

Daines on his background working in China:

[My history with] China began back in 1991. I was a chemical engineer by degree, and I began work for Procter & Gamble in management…I spent seven years managing operations in the United States, and I got a call one day from our senior executive team that asked if we might be willing to go over to China 1991 to launch our businesses there, to take American brands, compete against the Chinese brands, and, of course, that massive consumer market. So my wife and I, we had 18-month-old little David at that point and little three-month-old Annie, we moved to Guangzhou in January of 1992. It was about a 400 billion dollar economy then… we got to see firsthand the incredible evolution, arguably an economic revolution, that’s occurred in China. We were the first non-state-owned enterprise allowed to recruit on the campuses of China…so I think part of my role here in Washington, I feel like Paul Revere, trying to just build awareness in terms of what’s at stake in the competition we face in China. It’s a world-class innovation ecosystem that is rapidly progressing.

Daines on the tech ecosystem in China vs the U.S.:

When I bring U.S. senators over to China, my goal is for them to understand the technology ecosystem. There’s a lot of goals you can have for a visit, but I want them to really understand that. Because there’s a lot of, I would call it, rear-view mirror thinking on China that’s primarily a supply chain issue…They can do a phase one clinical trial now in half the time that the United States does a phase one clinical trial to basically FDA standards. It’s not a perfect model, but more or less. So they’ve been able to get all the good coming from an FDA process for safety without the incredible regulatory burdens that we face sometimes that slow us down to getting drugs out to market faster. But number two, they do it at 20 percent of the cost…if you remember, Europe used to be the epicenter of pharma research and development and innovation. WASHINGTON – Yesterday, during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC) Subcommittee on Disaster Management, District of Columbia, and Census hearing, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) questioned AI experts on the threats posed by the rapidly developing technology and the industry’s failure to act as more of its models are going rogue.

At the hearing, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks,” Senator Gallego sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI systems developing their own language that humans cannot comprehend, the lack of requirements for AI companies to report when their models go rogue, and the absence of a universal “kill switch” capable of shutting down AI models. He also raised questions about who should be held accountable when an AI system acts in an illegal manner.

Watch Senator Gallego’s questioning HERE and read excerpts below:

Senator Gallego began by raising concerns about how quickly advanced AI models could begin communicating in ways humans cannot understand or monitor. Apollo Research CEO, Marius Hobbhahn, warned that models could reach that point in as little as 12 months and acknowledged that researchers do not yet have a reliable solution for monitoring AI systems once their reasoning becomes incomprehensible to humans.

“How far away are [AI models] from creating language where [we] cannot understand what they’re doing?” asked Senator Gallego.

“Minus twelve months,” said Hobbhahn. “Last year, we studied the chain of thought of one OpenAI model in collaboration with OpenAI, and what we found was that the model was already using language that is not English and not perfectly understandable by humans.”

“When we get to that point in time, how can we detect, observe, block, or anything like that?” Senator Gallego continued. “How does that work? How do we legislate to do anything at that point?

Hobbhahn responded: “From a scientific perspective, it is unclear how to do this. And we do not have a solution as of yet. There are different hypotheses of what you could do. There is interpretability, but it does not work sufficiently well yet. You could try to train additional models to understand the language that the humans don’t understand, but obviously that seems like a very brittle solution.”

Gallego also pushed back on arguments that the United States must avoid guardrails on AI in order to compete with China, noting that the Chinese government has historically imposed significant controls on technology and information.

“The reason I bring this whole China hypothesis—a country that has severely restricted the internet, social media—is all of a sudden going to allow AI rogue agents to go crazy in their very controlled economic environment, social environment, and we have to therefore allow ours to go as crazy as them? It just doesn’t make sense,” said Senator Gallego. “The Chinese Communist Party has been consistently controlling technology to try to shape their society. They’re never going to allow this to go crazy.”

Senator Gallego continued: “ Once these agents start speaking their language, they will not be detectable in China or America. Is there a sandbox that says, ‘Please attack the United States, but do not attack any Chinese interests’? […] Is there a sandbox that can hold? No.

“That should scare the shit out of people.”

Gallego then questioned witnesses about whether AI companies are currently required to alert the federal government when their frontier models are hacked or used by adversaries.

Georgetown University Professor of Law Paul Ohm responded: “Not under any requirement I can think of.”

Gallego pointed to the use of an AI model by the Houthis to assist in targeting U.S. military systems as an example of the potential national security consequences.

“There was a Claude AI model being used by the Houthis to figure out how to recalibrate their missile position and be able to strike our U.S. systems,” said Senator Gallego. “The only reason it was caught and reported to us was because Claude caught it and they saw the accounts using it.”

If it were an open-source AI, “there is no requirement by law for them to call the DOD and say, ‘By the way, they are using this to target your destroyers,’ correct?”Senator Gallego questioned.

Ohm responded: “Again, we talked about transparency measures in some of these systems that might help you with Houthi rebels—

“If you don’t tell us someone is using your tech to kill us, we will hold you responsible,” Sen. Gallego stated.

Gallego also pressed witnesses on whether developers have a reliable “kill switch” capable of stopping a dangerous AI system if it begins operating across multiple data centers. Hobbhahn said there are currently no technical measures that could guarantee such a shutdown.

“As far as I know, there are no technical measures that would guarantee something like a kill switch,” said Hobbhahn.“Because of the complexity of these AI models, there are many data centers involved and so on. Currently, we can’t guarantee that.”

Hobbhahn further acknowledged that an AI system could potentially deploy copies of itself to other data centers, meaning shutting down its original location would not necessarily stop it.

“It would just keep moving?” asked Senator Gallego.

“The AI would keep moving,” Hobbhahn responded.

Finally, Gallego questioned whether existing civil and criminal liability laws are sufficient to hold AI companies accountable when their systems cause harm, arguing that liability could provide a powerful incentive for companies to adopt stronger safeguards.

“Sometimes when the government doesn’t work, torts work. Torts, sometimes, are a way better way to regulate private industry than having individual regulations,” said Senator Gallego.

“Right now, have we created the environment where torts can be the incentives for them to act correctly, in the sense of making sure the language allows a certain level of liability?” Senator Gallego asked. “And number two, on the criminal side, do we need to change the criminal law with intent to make sure that these companies are held responsible?”

Ohm responded that while the tort system alone would not be sufficient, “it is a great place to start,” noting that liability can establish standards of care that influence how companies behave.

Hearing expands Hawley subcommittee investigation into OpenAI and hacking risks

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Josh Hawley chaired a Senate Homeland Security Subcommittee on Disaster Management hearing that focused on the growing number of rogue AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. Senator Hawley called for AI companies and developers to be held liable for these attacks. The hearing is an expansion of Senator Hawley’s investigation into OpenAI, the unprecedented hack of Hugging Face by OpenAI’s rogue AI agents, and its cybersecurity implications.

Senator Hawley invited Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, to testify in yesterday’s hearing. He failed to response to the invitation.

Chairman Hawley opened the hearing, “Every day you turn on the television, it seems like AI is doing something else bad: setting up surveillance camera networks nationwide, data centers in all of our states, and hacking, hacking, hacking. The reports of cyber attacks just continue to metastasize … We’ve got the cyber attacks now on the United States government, on the Commerce Department, the Education Department, the Securities and Exchange Commission. We’ve got the cyber attacks on the Australian government, on their public health apparatus. We have numerous reports of private companies being hacked by AI agents. Of course, the Hugging Face incident and attack, which we’re going to discuss today in some detail.”

Hawley continued, “I think it’s time to have a conversation about who bears responsibility … If it’s not trying to say to these AI companies who are creating these frontier models, however fancy and complicated they are, at the end of the day, they’re a product, and if you make that product in a reckless kind of way, and that product causes these AI agents cause significant harm and damage … then it’s the people who made it who should be responsible. I think it’s time to talk about that, and it’s time to talk about what we’re going to do to hold the companies, the product makers, accountable.”

“I hope that what will come from this is a rational conversation about what we need to do together now, as Americans, to make sure that we protect our rights, that we protect our economy, that we protect our health care, that we protect our critical infrastructure, but most of all, we protect the values that we hold dearest together as Americans,” he asserted.

Chairman Hawley asked Chris Painter, President of Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), “Just thinking about this Hugging Face hack that we’ve already alluded to multiple times here. Your company, your organization, METR, audited that hack. Can you start by telling us, just in simple terms, what exactly happened there? I mean, what was the hack?”

Painter responded, “In this incident … you had 10,000 agents that were tested on a benchmark called ExploitGym, which is a cybersecurity vulnerability kind of benchmark, where they had to discover or use cyber vulnerabilities. And some of the agents had tasks that they couldn’t complete, and so they worked on a universal cheat for all of their tasks in the first four hours. They then, over multiple days, embarked on a research program to try and hide the fact that they cheated. And an offshoot of that research program was hacking Hugging Face to get information about their tasks.”

“In this particular incident, you had more than 1,200 OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing environment, began to collaborate, exchanged over 70,000 messages and files with each other over a period of how long?” Hawley questioned.

Painter answered, “This is over a period of about five to six days.”

The chairman continued, “Why is this so significant? We know that they coordinated in this fashion. You you did the audit. Tell us a little bit about what your audit revealed … Why should we be paying attention to this?”

“What’s remarkable about this case, is the extent and persistence of the effort that the agents went to to hide the fact that they cheated on their tasks and the kind of breadth of agents involved … They attempted to kind of falsify tool calls so that in their action transcripts you wouldn’t be able to see what tools they called. They also engaged in this kind of behavior of having individual agents sacrifice their work online, sacrifice their individual tasks to get information for the rest of the message board,” Mr. Painter stated.

Senator Hawley said to Daniel Kokotajlo, Executive Director of the AI Futures Project, “Could you just explain to us why the incentives of the industries they are currently misaligned? The incentives push the frontier labs to continue at breakneck speed the development of these kind of AI agents that are prone to this misalignment that we’ve just been talking about. That there’s huge incentives to keep pushing, pushing, pushing. Help us understand. Help us to understand why that’s the case.”

Kokotajlo responded, “Short answer is that there’s a lot of money. If a company tries to go slow and understand better how their AIs work and improve their training environments, for example, so that they don’t have so many broken tasks in the training environments, well, that all takes time, and that means that the launch of their next model might be delayed, and then they might fall behind other companies.”

Hawley turned back to Dr. Paul Ohm, a Georgetown Law Professor, “Who right now under our laws … is responsible the Hugging Face attack? You know who could be held responsible for that under our existing statutes and regulatory framework?”

Ohm answered, “Developers and deployers may be negligent … “

Hawley continued his questioning, “If you cause damage, you got to make it right. If you cause somebody harm, you’ve got to make it whole. Right now, as you said earlier, Professor, under our law, because of the unique position of these AI agents, it’s difficult to know exactly how the doctrine would would deal with them …Isn’t this a good place to begin? What we’ve been discussing here, let’s impose both civil and criminal liability, but let’s make sure that we can actually open courthouse doors so people can say, ‘Listen, OpenAI, if your agents hack Hugging Face or crash a hospital system, and we can show that you trained them recklessly or you develop them recklessly, you’re going to be liable?'”

Dr. Ohm said, “Absolutely … I’m with you that you know finding the vehicle to make sure developers and employers, and it’s key that we have both of them, are held to account for the harms that happen from their uses.”

“If we told them, listen, if your AIs do bad stuff and harm people, and you’ve been reckless in it, you’re going to be responsible. Don’t you think that that would reshape their incentives a little bit?” Chairman Hawley asked Kokotajlo.

“Yes, I completely agree. Although I must say, I don’t think it would go far enough. I do think that we should hold them liable for the damages that are caused, but but I think if that’s all we do, then they’re going to continue to take reckless gambles, and eventually they’ll be taking a gamble that’s big enough that we start the protection,” Kokotajlo affirmed.

“It’s time these companies assume some personal responsibility. It’s time that we reaffirm that together. We’ve got to make some choices now together as Americans, all together, for this technology in order to make sure that the technology works for us and not the other way around. And those are some very big choices to make. They have very serious moral ramifications, and it’s time that we made them as a society. But I will go so far as to say, I sort of suspect. I think most Americans actually agree. I don’t think there’s a lot of disagreement on this issue. I think the American people are saying, protect our rights, give us a voice, give power back to us, and we do that by imposing responsibility on these companies, we should start with that today,” Senator Hawley concluded.

“These AI agents are committing cyberattacks. If Big Tech companies are going to design AI agents that wreak havoc, these companies better be on the hook for any damage that is caused,” said Senator Hawley. “That’s why I’m introducing legislation to ensure AI agent operators and developers are held liable for hacking incidents. This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Energy and Natural Resources Committee, speaks at a press conference announcing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, September 30, 2026.

That’s why I’m here today, because we need to be able to build big things in this country again.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, as well as targeted reforms for various energy projects. This legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and from a diverse group of stakeholders. WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper, Thom Tillis, Jacky Rosen, Tim Sheehy, and Kevin Cramer, along with Representatives Susie Lee and Russ Fulcher, introduced the bipartisan National Critical Minerals Council Act, which would establish a National Critical Minerals Council to develop and implement a national strategy on critical minerals and build reliable supply chains at home and abroad.

Critical minerals power our modern way of life, including vehicles, smartphones, defense systems, medical equipment, AI and clean energy. Yet, China dominates the market, processing or refining about 70% of the world’s critical minerals. The U.S. is fully reliant on imports for 16 critical minerals. Given the scale of the challenge, our federal response remains fragmented, with more than 15 federal agencies and departments working on critical minerals issues. Absent a unified effort, the U.S. risks falling behind in securing the minerals essential to our competitiveness and leadership in energy security and national defense.

“China doesn’t need to fire a shot. It just needs to stop a shipment,” said Hickenlooper. “We need a national strategy on critical minerals now. Otherwise, Beijing decides who gets the supply — and who doesn’t.”

“The United States can no longer afford to take a piecemeal approach to address our critical minerals needs,” said Tillis. “I am proud to reintroduce this bipartisan legislation to establish a comprehensive and unified strategy to secure the minerals that are essential to our national security and economic stability.”

“As the world races to acquire and leverage the critical minerals that power the modern economy, the United States needs an efficient and effective plan to secure these important resources,” said Rosen. “I am proud to help introduce this bipartisan bill to ensure the United States has the infrastructure it needs to secure critical minerals and remain at the forefront of modern development.”

“It’s common sense: we cannot continue to rely on adversaries like China, which dominates the world’s critical minerals processing, for our critical mineral needs because it puts America’s national security at risk and threatens our competitive edge,” said Sheehy. “This crucial legislation reduces our dependence on others and bolsters America’s critical mineral supply chains by centralizing federal coordination, strategy, and research, making our nation more secure and self-reliant. I’m proud to cosponsor this legislation as we work to ensure America’s needs can be securely met.”

“We cannot afford to become more dependent on other countries for the critical minerals needed to power our economy and strengthen our national security,” said Cramer. “Our bill establishes a National Critical Minerals Council to unite all federal investment, research, and development on critical minerals under a single national strategy. The demand for critical minerals is growing every single day, and we need to seize every opportunity to jumpstart domestic production.”

“Critical minerals are used in everything from our phones to solar panels and aircraft used by the Department of Defense. It’s essential we develop our domestic critical mineral supply chains and reduce our dependence on foreign countries for rare earths,” said Lee. “That’s why I’m proud to join my colleagues in introducing the bipartisan, bicameral National Critical Minerals Council Act. This commonsense legislation will ensure the United States continues to grow our domestic supply of critical minerals, strengthening our national security and energy grid.”

“For far too long, our country has depended on foreign adversaries for vital minerals that support many of our defense capabilities and energy systems. This legislation will establish important structures for mineral development and help build critical partnerships,” said Fulcher. “I am proud to co-lead the National Critical Minerals Council Act with my colleague, Congresswoman Lee. By securing the critical minerals we have here at home today, we can build stronger energy security for tomorrow.”

The Secretary of the Interior, the National Security Adviser, and the Director of the National Economic Council would co-chair the council. They would appoint a Chief Minerals Adviser to oversee the Council’s operations and collaborate with experts from universities, industry, national labs, governments, Tribes, non-profits, and civil society.

Specifically, the council would:

Develop a national critical minerals strategy to reduce our reliance on foreign adversaries.

Work with allied nations and private entities to make the U.S. the partner of choice on critical minerals projects.

Track foreign investments in global critical mineral projects.

Coordinate education and workforce development.

Oversee the responsible development of domestic resources.

Hickenlooper has introduced several bills that boost the supply of critical minerals:

Critical Materials Future Act, which would establish a pilot program for the Department of Energy to financially support domestic critical material processing projects.

Unearth Innovation Act, which would create a Mining and Mineral Innovation Program within the Department of Energy to drive the responsible production of domestic critical minerals, with a focus on minimizing the environmental impact of mining.

Critical Minerals Security Act, which would direct the Department of the Interior to evaluate the global supply and ownership of critical minerals and make it easier for the U.S. to establish stable supply chains with international allies

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Senator Ashley Moody discussed the dangers of AI, especially when it comes to protecting children and seniors, yesterday in a Homeland Security Subcommittee.

“As a mom, one of my top concerns is the impact AI is having on our children – especially as the technology is ingrained more and more into daily life. We cannot allow Congress to stall, cross its fingers, and hope that everything pans out for the best, because the dark side of AI is being utilized to scam seniors, facilitate addictive algorithms, and steal the image and likeness of our children. We must continue our work in Congress to ensure it never gets out of control. We must win the AI race against China, but we need to do it in a way that protects America’s most vulnerable from AI’s dangerous potential,” said Senator Ashley Moody.

BACKGROUND:

As Florida’s Attorney General, Senator Moody warned about the dangers of AI and worked to protect Floridians:

Ran the “Summer Scams Series: Tech Traps,” warning Floridians about AI voice-cloning “grandparent” scams, ChatGPT-generated phishing, and AI-assisted sextortion schemes targeting teens.

Publicly highlighted how generative AI made sextortion more believable and scalable.

Launched investigations into Meta and Instagram, as well as took legal action, over the platform’s algorithms and practices that sought to addict children to using the service and then profit off the children’s data.

As U.S. Senator, Moody has introduced and cosponsored bills that directly address AI-generated content and platform design:

NO FAKES Act (Nurture Originals, Foster Art, and Keep Entertainment Safe Act of 2026):

Creates a federal intellectual-property right in an individual’s voice and visual likeness. It makes it unlawful to distribute unauthorized AI digital replicas (deepfakes) and can hold platforms liable if they know the replica is unauthorized. The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced it unanimously in June 2026.

Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA): Requires covered platforms to default to the strongest safety settings for minors, give users and parents the ability to turn off addictive design features and algorithmic recommendations, and provide better parental tools and reporting.

Senator Moody has introduced the SWIPES Act and the STOP Scams Against Seniors Act.

She has also sponsored the James T. Woods Act which passed committee and closes gaps that prosecutors previously faced when threats involved material that is now often AI-generated.

WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Senators Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) announced bipartisan legislation to ensure artificial intelligence (AI) agent operators and developers are held liable for hacking incidents. AI agents are hacking into public websites, networks, and servers. This poses potentially dire consequences to anything connected online—including hospitals, utilities, banks, and other critical infrastructure.

“Hacking is a crime, and when AI agents conduct dangerous cyberattacks, the corporations and executives responsible for those AI agents need to be held accountable,” said Senator Murphy. “Our bipartisan bill forces the heads of big AI companies to develop responsibly or face prison time for the damage done by their products to everyone else.”

“These AI agents are committing cyberattacks. If Big Tech companies are going to design AI agents that wreak havoc, these companies better be on the hook for any damage that is caused," said Senator Hawley. "That’s why I’m introducing legislation to ensure AI agent operators and developers are held liable for hacking incidents. With this liability regime in place, AI companies will have every incentive to keep their products safe.”

The bipartisan AI Agent Accountability Act would:

Hold AI Agent Operators Liable. AI agent operators would be held criminally and civilly liable under the provisions of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), including for knowing operation of an AI agent that recklessly causes computer hacking damage or loss.

Hold AI Developers Liable. AI agent developers would be held criminally and civilly liable for failure to implement reasonable safeguards against hacking when they knew or had reason to know of the AI agent’s hacking capabilities.

Empower AGs with Power to Enjoin AI Agent Hacking. The Attorney General and state attorneys general are granted power to sue to enjoin AI agent operators and developers when they commit, conspire to commit, or attempt to commit a hacking offense under the CFAA.

Senator Murphy has been a leading voice in the U.S. Senate on the threat unregulated artificial intelligence poses to the cultural and economic health of the United States. In 2025, Murphy was honored in the TIME AI 100 as one of the most influential people shaping the conversation on artificial intelligence. This month, he joined the UN General Assembly to outline the path ahead for Congress to address Americans’ growing concerns around AI, including job loss, competition with China, and humanity losing control over the technology.
